title: The Forgotten Voices of Project Follow Through
author: Olivia Chilkoti
summary: Olivia Chilkoti reports on Project Follow Through, the 1968 to 1977 federal experiment that compared teaching approaches across US elementary schools and found Direct Instruction produced the strongest results. Critics dismissed the approach as strict and authoritarian, but the children who experienced it have rarely been heard. APM Reports interviewed seven former students from Johnson School in East St. Louis, who remember their teacher Ruby Hudson and the program fondly. They recall fast-paced, small-group lessons, games, a stable three-year relationship with one teacher, no corporal punishment, and supports such as dental checkups and summer trips. The early test scores surprised even the program's creators, who sent new testers to confirm them. Former students describe the years after Follow Through as a decline, and the story contends that their accounts challenge common criticisms of Direct Instruction.
points: The story supplies the missing student perspective on Follow Through, a debate previously carried on by researchers, policymakers, and educators.
Former students describe scripted, fast-paced Direct Instruction as fun and encouraging, which contradicts the charge that it was joyless or authoritarian.
Small skill-based groups did not make children feel singled out, and keeping the same teacher for three years let her target each child's weak spots.
Test scores were so high that the program's directors had new testers repeat the exams, and the results held.
The students' sharp decline in later schools shows how much the surrounding school environment matters to what children carry forward.
